web-7d9f5b4c6-abc12     1/1     Running   0          2d    10.0.1.15    node-1

title: Apply configuration
description: Apply a configuration file to create or update Kubernetes resources declaratively.

breakdown.meaning: Apply a configuration to a resource
Specify the file containing the configuration

flags.description: Filename, directory, or URL to files to apply

output:
deployment.apps/web created
service/web-service created
tip: Always use 'kubectl apply' over 'kubectl create' for reproducible, declarative deployments. Use '--dry-run=client -o yaml' to preview.

tip: Use 'kubectl logs -l app=web' to get logs from all pods matching a label. Add '--previous' to see logs from a crashed container.

title: Scale a deployment
description: Change the number of replicas for a Deployment, ReplicaSet, or StatefulSet — the primary way to scale workloads up or down.

breakdown.meaning: Set a new size for a resource

example: kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5 && kubectl get pods -l app=web
output:
deployment.apps/web scaled
NAME                   READY   STATUS    AGE
web-7d9f5b4c6-abc12   1/1     Running   2d
web-7d9f5b4c6-def34   1/1     Running   2d
web-7d9f5b4c6-ghi56   1/1     Running   5s
web-7d9f5b4c6-jkl78   1/1     Running   5s
web-7d9f5b4c6-mno90   0/1     Pending   2s
tip: Use HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) for automatic scaling based on CPU/memory metrics.

flags.description: The new desired number of replicas
Specify the namespace scope for this request
Only scale if current replicas match this value
Wait this long for the operation to complete

title: Execute command in pod
description: Open an interactive shell session inside a running pod container for debugging or inspection.

breakdown.meaning: Execute a command in a container

output:
Defaulted container "web" out of: web, sidecar
/ # ls
bin   dev   etc   home  proc  root  sys   tmp   usr   var

tip: Use '/bin/bash' instead of '/bin/sh' if the container has bash installed. For a quick one-off command, skip '-it' and just run: 'kubectl exec pod-name -- cat /etc/config'.

title: Delete resources
description: Delete Kubernetes resources defined in a configuration file, removing pods, services, and other objects.

breakdown.meaning: Specify the file that defines the resources to delete

flags.description: Filename, directory, or URL to files containing resources to delete
Seconds to wait before force deletion (-1 for default, 0 for immediate)
Immediately remove resources from API and bypass graceful deletion
Filter resources by label selector
Delete all resources of the specified type in the namespace
Cascade deletion to dependents (default true)

output:
deployment.apps "web" deleted
service "web-service" deleted
tip: Use '--dry-run=client' to preview what would be deleted before actually deleting. To delete a stuck resource, try '--grace-period=0 --force'. Be careful with '--all' in production namespaces.

command: kubectl rollout status deployment/web && kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
title: Manage rollouts
description: Check the status of a deployment rollout, and if needed, undo it to roll back to the previous revision.

breakdown.meaning: Watch the rollout progress of a resource
Run next command only if the first succeeds
Roll back to the previous deployment revision
Target the same deployment for rollback

flags.description: Roll back to a specific revision number
Watch the status of the rollout until complete (default true for status)
Timeout for waiting on rollout status (e.g. 5m0s)
Specify the namespace scope for this request

example: kubectl rollout status deployment/web && kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
output:
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
deployment.apps/web rolled back
tip: Use 'kubectl rollout history deployment/web' to see all revisions. Roll back to a specific version with '--to-revision=2'. Combine with 'kubectl rollout pause' and 'kubectl rollout resume' for canary-style deployments.

title: Port forward to pod
description: Forward a local port to a port on a pod, allowing you to access pod services from your local machine.

breakdown.meaning: Forward local ports to a pod
Map local port 8080 to pod port 80

flags.description: Addresses to listen on (default localhost, use 0.0.0.0 for all interfaces)
Specify the namespace scope for this request
Timeout for waiting for at least one pod to be running

output:
Forwarding from 127.0.0.1:8080 -> 80
Forwarding from [::1]:8080 -> 80
Handling connection for 8080
tip: You can also port-forward to a service with 'kubectl port-forward svc/web-service 8080:80'. Use '&' to run in the background. To listen on all interfaces, add '--address 0.0.0.0'.

title: Switch context/namespace
description: Switch the active Kubernetes context to target a different cluster or environment.

breakdown.meaning: Set the current context in kubeconfig
Name of the context to switch to

flags.description: Path to a specific kubeconfig file to use
Set the default namespace for the context (with set-context)
Set the cluster for the context (with set-context)
Set the user for the context (with set-context)

output: Switched to context "production".
tip: Use 'kubectl config get-contexts' to list all available contexts. Set a default namespace with 'kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=my-namespace' to avoid typing '-n' every time. Consider using 'kubectx' and 'kubens' tools for faster switching.

flags.description: Specify the namespace scope for this request
Sort output by cpu or memory

Filter pods by label selector
Do not print header row

output:
NAME                     CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
api-6b8c4d5e7-ghi56     250m         512Mi

web-7d9f5b4c6-def34     95m          248Mi

title: Create secret
description: Create a Kubernetes secret imperatively from literal key-value pairs for storing sensitive data like passwords.

breakdown.meaning: Name of the secret to create

flags.description: Specify a key=value pair to insert into the secret (can be repeated)
Create secret from a file (key defaults to filename)
Create secret from an env-style file of key=value pairs
Secret type (e.g. Opaque, kubernetes.io/tls, kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson)
Specify the namespace scope for this request
Preview the secret without creating it

output: secret/db-creds created
tip: Secrets are base64-encoded, NOT encrypted by default. Use '--dry-run=client -o yaml' to generate a YAML manifest for version control (after encrypting with tools like SOPS or Sealed Secrets). For TLS secrets, use 'kubectl create secret tls' instead.

title: Get all resources
description: List the most common resource types in a namespace — pods, services, deployments, and replicasets — in a single command.

breakdown.meaning: List pods, services, deployments, replicasets, and more

flags.description: Target namespace
Show resources across all namespaces
Show additional columns like node and IP

example:
kubectl get all -n default
kubectl get all -A
kubectl get all -n production -o wide
output:
NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
pod/web-6d4cf56db6-xk2pq     1/1     Running   0

NAME          TYPE        CLUSTER-IP
service/web   ClusterIP   10.96.0.1
tip: Note that --all-namespaces with 'all' shows common types only, not CRDs. For truly all resources use 'kubectl api-resources --verbs=list' piped to kubectl get.

title: List cluster nodes
description: List all nodes in the cluster with their status, roles, age, and Kubernetes version — the starting point for cluster health checks.

breakdown.meaning: List all nodes in the cluster
Show extra columns: internal IP, OS, kernel version

flags.description: Show extra columns including IPs and OS
Show all node labels

example:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node my-node
output:
NAME        STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
node-1      Ready    control-plane   10d   v1.28.0
node-2      Ready    <none>          10d   v1.28.0
tip: Use '-o wide' to see node IPs and OS images. Run 'kubectl describe node nodename' for detailed resource capacity, taints, and conditions.

title: List services
description: List all services in a namespace showing their type, cluster IP, external IP, and exposed ports.

breakdown.meaning: List all services (svc is the short form)

flags.description: Target namespace
All namespaces
Show selector column

example:
kubectl get svc
kubectl get svc -n production
kubectl get svc -A
output:
NAME         TYPE           CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)
web          LoadBalancer   10.96.0.1       203.0.113.10    80:30080/TCP
db           ClusterIP      10.96.0.2       <none>          5432/TCP
tip: Use '-o wide' to see selector labels. Check EXTERNAL-IP for LoadBalancer services — it shows 'pending' until the cloud provider assigns one.

title: View cluster events
description: Show cluster events sorted by time — often the fastest way to understand why a pod is failing or stuck in a pending state.

breakdown.meaning: List events recorded by the cluster

flags.description: Sort by most recent
Show only warning events

example:
kubectl get events -n default --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
kubectl get events -n production --field-selector type=Warning
output:
LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON      OBJECT         MESSAGE
2m          Warning   BackOff     pod/web-xyz    Back-off restarting failed container
1m          Normal    Pulled      pod/web-xyz    Pulled image nginx:latest
tip: Filter to a specific pod or namespace: 'kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=mypod'. Events expire after ~1 hour, so check promptly after an incident.

title: List deployments
description: List all deployments in a namespace with replica counts, availability status, and rollout age.

flags.description: Target namespace
All namespaces
Show container images and selectors

example:
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get deployments -n production
kubectl get deploy -o wide
output:
NAME    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
web     3/3     3            3           5d
api     2/2     2            2           5d
tip: Check AVAILABLE vs READY columns for rollout problems. Use 'kubectl rollout status deploy/name' for a blocking wait and 'kubectl rollout history deploy/name' for change history.

title: Create a namespace
description: Create a new Kubernetes namespace — namespaces are virtual clusters within a cluster that isolate resources, letting teams or environments share the same infrastructure safely.

breakdown.meaning: The name for the new namespace

flags.description: Create a namespace imperatively
Generate YAML manifest without creating — good for GitOps workflows
Delete a namespace and ALL resources within it
List all namespaces in the cluster

output: namespace/production created
tip: Prefer declarative YAML for namespaces in production so they are tracked in git. Use kubectl create namespace name --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns.yaml to generate the YAML, then apply it with kubectl apply -f ns.yaml.

command: kubectl set image deployment/api api=registry.example.com/api:v2.1.0 -n production
title: Update deployment image
description: Update the container image used by a running deployment, triggering a rolling update — the standard way to deploy a new application version without downtime.

breakdown.meaning: Update the image reference in a workload resource
Container name (api) = new image and tag to deploy

flags.description: Target a deployment
Target a daemonset
Record the command in the rollout history (deprecated but still widely used)
Watch the rolling update progress
Roll back to the previous image if the update fails

output:
deployment.apps/api image updated
Waiting for deployment "api" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
deployment "api" successfully rolled out
tip: After updating, watch the rollout with kubectl rollout status deployment/NAME. If the new version has a problem, roll back instantly with kubectl rollout undo deployment/NAME. Always use an explicit image tag (never :latest) so rollbacks are deterministic.

title: Drain a node for maintenance
description: Safely evict all pods from a node before taking it offline for maintenance — pods are rescheduled to other nodes, and the node is marked as unschedulable.

breakdown.meaning: Evict all evictable pods from a node and mark it unschedulable
The name of the node to drain
Skip DaemonSet-managed pods — they cannot be evicted and run on every node by design
Allow eviction of pods using emptyDir volumes (local data will be lost)

flags.description: Required if DaemonSets exist on the node
Evict pods with emptyDir volumes (data is lost)
Evict pods not managed by a controller (they will not be rescheduled)
Override pod termination grace period in seconds
Mark the node schedulable again after maintenance

output:
node/node01 cordoned
evicting pod default/web-7d9f4b8c5-x2p9q
evicting pod default/api-6c8f5d9b4-r3k7m
node/node01 drained
tip: After maintenance, run kubectl uncordon node01 to allow pods to be scheduled on the node again. Use kubectl cordon NODE if you just want to stop new pods scheduling without evicting existing ones.

command: kubectl auth can-i create pods --namespace production
title: Check RBAC permissions
description: Verify whether the current user or service account has permission to perform a specific Kubernetes action — essential for debugging RBAC access denied errors.

breakdown.meaning: Check whether an action is allowed by RBAC policy
The verb (create) and resource (pods) to check
Check permission within this specific namespace

flags.description: Check permissions in a specific namespace
Impersonate another user to test their permissions
Impersonate a group
List all actions you can perform in a namespace
Check sub-resource access: --subresource=log (for pod/log)

output: yes
tip: Use --as to test another user's permissions: kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:production:my-sa. Use --list to see all allowed actions in a namespace without guessing individual verbs.
